segments.text: This is the Eurofighter Typhoon, a twin-engine fighter that was designed above all for air combat.
Its original mission was pretty clear.
Intercept threats, climb fast, build speed, and take on other fighters in the air.
But over time, the Typhoon evolved.
It stopped being just an air combat specialist and gradually took on missions against targets on the ground as well.
On the other side, we have the Dassault Raphael.
And from the beginning, the idea behind the Raphael was a little different.
It was designed as a more versatile do-it-all fighter.
It can handle air-to-air combat, precision strikes, anti-ship missions, and in its naval version,
it can even operate directly from an aircraft carrier.
So, we're talking about two of the most important combat aircraft ever produced in Europe.
But what's interesting is that even though they compete for many of the same contracts today,
they came from very different ideas.
The Typhoon grew out of a joint program involving four European countries.
The Raphael, on the other hand, was developed essentially by France after Paris decided to go its own way.
Today, the two fighters compete for multi-billion dollar contracts,
and they represent two very different approaches to developing, upgrading, and selling a modern combat aircraft.
And to make this comparison as fair as possible, I had to decide exactly which versions we're going to use.

especially upgraded Tranche 2 and Tranche 3 aircraft,

the single-seat land-based version in the F3R standard,
